introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2025. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées d'après les notions classiques du programme de Géologie A Level, sans source consultable. Question 4(a) : compositions, textures et modes de gisement des trois roches (péridotite, dolérite, rhyolite) donnés d'après les manuels (pourcentages de silice et de minéraux en ordres de grandeur). La péridotite est aussi la roche du manteau supérieur : le corrigé le précise car son « taux de refroidissement » n'a de sens que pour les péridotites d'intrusions et de complexes ophiolitiques.

Question 4(b) : les exemples de gisements de type placer et d'enrichissement supergène sont des exemples classiques de manuel (étain alluvial de Malaisie, or du Klondike, sables à minéraux lourds, cuivre porphyrique du Chili) ; aucun fait local (Cameroun) n'est affirmé.
Points : 12 + 8 + 5 = 25, conformes au sujet ; les sous-questions (b)(i) et (b)(ii) portent ensemble les 8 points imprimés.

questions.corrige_markdown:
| Heading | **Peridotite** | **Dolerite** | **Rhyolite** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(i) Composition** | **Ultrabasic (ultramafic)**, less than about 45 per cent $\mathrm{SiO_2}$. Mainly **olivine (over 40 per cent)** with **pyroxene (augite, orthopyroxene)**; accessory chromite, magnetite, some amphibole or garnet. **No quartz and no feldspar.** Dark green to black, very dense. | **Basic (mafic)**, about 45 to 52 per cent $\mathrm{SiO_2}$. About half **calcium-rich plagioclase (labradorite)** and a third **augite**, with some olivine and iron-titanium oxides (magnetite, ilmenite). | **Acid (felsic)**, more than about 69 per cent $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ (70 to 77). **Quartz, alkali feldspar (orthoclase, sanidine)** and sodium-rich plagioclase, with a little biotite or hornblende. It is the volcanic equivalent of **granite**. Light coloured (pink, grey, cream). |
| **(ii) Texture** | **Coarse-grained (phaneritic)**, granular and equigranular; crystals interlock (sometimes **cumulate** texture in layered bodies). | **Medium-grained**, often **ophitic or sub-ophitic**: laths of plagioclase are partly or wholly enclosed in larger crystals of augite. It may be porphyritic. | **Fine-grained (aphanitic) or glassy**, often **porphyritic** (phenocrysts of quartz and feldspar in a fine groundmass); **flow banding**, spherulites or vesicles may occur. |
| **(iii) Rate of cooling** | **Very slow**, deep in the crust (plutonic intrusions), which gives large crystals; (peridotite of the mantle has an even longer history). | **Intermediate (moderately fast)**: it cools faster than a plutonic rock but more slowly than lava, as it crystallises at **shallow depth (hypabyssal)**, so the crystals are of medium size. | **Rapid**, at or near the Earth's surface in contact with air, water or cold rock, which gives very small crystals or glass. |
| **(iv) Field occurrence** | In **layered intrusions** (for example the Bushveld and Stillwater complexes), in **ophiolite complexes (oceanic crust and upper mantle slices)**, in alpine-type bodies, and as **xenoliths in basalt and kimberlite**. It is easily serpentinised, and weathers to laterite (nickel ores). | **Minor intrusions: dykes and sills** (for example the Whin Sill in England), and also in volcanic necks; **chilled margins** against the country rock and **columnar jointing** are common; it weathers with a spheroidal pattern. | **Lava flows, domes and plugs**, and **pyroclastic deposits (ignimbrites, ash flows)** in continental volcanic areas and in association with granite plutons; also as thin dykes. |

*Summary:* peridotite is a **plutonic ultrabasic** rock, dolerite a **hypabyssal basic** rock and rhyolite an **extrusive acid** rock, so composition and cooling rate (and therefore texture) both change from one to the other.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Using examples, briefly describe the following:

(i) Placer deposits;

(ii) Supergene enrichment deposits.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Placer deposits.** A **placer** is a **mechanical concentration of heavy, hard and chemically resistant minerals**, released from their source rocks by weathering and erosion, by **running water (rivers: alluvial placers)**, **waves (beach placers)** or sometimes wind. The valuable minerals are **dense** and **do not decompose**, so they settle first where the **velocity of the water falls**: on the **inside of river bends (point bars)**, behind bedrock bars and in pot-holes, at the foot of rapids, and on beaches where the waves sort the sand. Light minerals (quartz, clay) are washed away. Gold nuggets and grains, diamonds, cassiterite, platinum, ilmenite, rutile, zircon, monazite and magnetite are commonly found in placers. *Examples:* **alluvial gold** of the Klondike river gravels (Yukon, Canada); **alluvial tin (cassiterite)** of Malaysia and Indonesia; **alluvial diamonds** of the Orange River and the coast of Namibia; **beach sand deposits of ilmenite, rutile and zircon** in eastern Australia and India. They are mined cheaply by dredging, panning or sluicing.

**(ii) Supergene enrichment deposits.** **Supergene enrichment** is the **secondary enrichment of the metal content of an ore body near the surface by descending (downward-moving) groundwater**, after **weathering** of the primary (hypogene) sulphide ore. The process is as follows:

1. Above the water table, **oxygenated rain water oxidises the primary sulphides** (for example chalcopyrite and pyrite), which gives **acid solutions** containing dissolved metal sulphates (copper sulphate). The leached, iron-stained residual cap is the **gossan (iron hat)**.
2. These solutions **move down** and, below the **water table** (in reducing conditions), react with the primary sulphides and **precipitate the metal as secondary sulphides** such as **chalcocite ($\mathrm{Cu_2S}$) and covellite ($\mathrm{CuS}$)**, which are richer in copper than the original minerals.
3. This forms a **blanket (zone of secondary enrichment)** of high-grade ore just below the water table, and the **primary low-grade ore** remains beneath it.

*Example:* the **porphyry copper deposits** of **Chile** (for example Chuquicamata and Escondida) and of south-western USA, where the supergene chalcocite blanket makes the deposit economic. (Supergene enrichment of iron, manganese and gold ores also occurs.) The zones from top to bottom are: gossan or leached cap, zone of oxidation, zone of secondary enrichment, primary ore.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Outline the methods that can be used to prevent landslides.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **landslide** happens when the **shear stress** on a slope is greater than the **shear strength** of its material. Prevention aims to **reduce the driving forces** and **increase the resisting forces**:

1. **Drainage of water** (the most important method): **surface drains and ditches** to divert run-off away from the slope, **sub-surface drains and weep holes** to lower the water table and reduce the pore-water pressure; waterproofing of cracks and avoiding leaking pipes and soakaways on the slope.
2. **Reducing the slope angle and the load:** **grading the slope to a gentler angle**, **cutting benches (terraces)**, and removing material from the top of the slope; avoiding building or dumping heavy loads at the head.
3. **Retaining structures at the base:** **retaining walls, gabions, piles and buttresses** or a **rock fill at the toe** to support the slope (**counterweight**), and protection of the toe from undercutting by rivers or waves.
4. **Reinforcing the slope:** **rock bolts, anchors, soil nailing and grouting**, **shotcrete and wire mesh** (nets) on rock faces, and rock-fall barriers.
5. **Vegetation:** planting **trees and grass** whose roots bind the soil and take up water; prevention of **deforestation** and of overgrazing.
6. **Land-use control and monitoring:** hazard mapping and zoning (no building on unstable ground), avoiding undercutting the slope by excavation or road cuts, and **monitoring** with inclinometers and extensometers and **early warning** systems.
